findings.title: Alabama Becomes 21st State to Enact Comprehensive Privacy Law
findings.source: IAPP U.S. Privacy Digest / IAPP News
findings.summary: Alabama's House Bill 351, the Alabama Personal Data Protection Act, cleared the state legislature on April 7, 2026, making Alabama the 21st state to pass a comprehensive consumer privacy law. The bill applies to businesses controlling or processing data of more than 25,000 Alabama residents or deriving 25% of revenue from data sales. If signed by the governor, the law takes effect May 1, 2027, and grants consumers rights to confirm processing, correct inaccuracies, delete data, obtain a copy, and opt out of targeted advertising. The bill includes notable departures from the standard state privacy law template, including unique applicability thresholds and entity-level exemptions.

findings.title: Maine's Comprehensive Privacy Bill Fails on Final House Vote
findings.source: IAPP Daily Dashboard / IAPP U.S. Privacy Digest
findings.summary: The Maine Legislature will not finalize comprehensive privacy legislation before the end of its current legislative session on April 15, the Maine Morning Star reports. The House voted against concurrence on Legislative Document 1822, the Maine Online Data Privacy Act, for the second time in a week, ultimately ending the bill's consideration during the current session. The House and Senate had been debating a controversial political organizations exemption before local industry groups made a final lobbying push to sway a majority of House lawmakers against the bill.

findings.title: New AI Model Sparks Alarm as Governments Brace for AI-Driven Cyberattacks
findings.summary: Governments and stakeholders worldwide are contemplating how frontier AI model capabilities could be exploited by threat actors, as Anthropic's Claude Mythos model raises new cybersecurity concerns. Questions are emerging about how cybersecurity practices will remain resilient in the face of evolving AI models. Governments across multiple jurisdictions are assessing the implications for critical infrastructure and national security.

findings.title: A View from DC: The Federal Plan to Modernize and Preempt Financial Privacy Rules
findings.source: IAPP Daily Dashboard / On the Ground—U.S.
findings.summary: House lawmakers are advancing plans to address financial data privacy via proposed amendments to the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act. The proposals aim to modernize and potentially preempt state-level financial privacy rules, representing a significant shift in the federal approach to financial sector data protection.

findings.title: CalPrivacy Seeks Stakeholder Feedback on DROP Audits
findings.source: IAPP U.S. Privacy Digest / Law & Regulation
findings.summary: The California Privacy Protection Agency is seeking stakeholder comments on Delete Request and Opt-Out Platform audits as it looks to propose regulations defining audit requirements for data brokers. CalPrivacy is soliciting feedback on potential credential requirements for third-party auditors, audit standards, and potential AI and security safeguards. The comment deadline is May 7, 2026.

findings.title: US Appeals Court Holds BIPA Amendment Can Be Applied to Pending Cases
findings.source: IAPP U.S. Privacy Digest / Law & Regulation
findings.summary: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit upheld a lower court ruling affirming that the 2024 amendment to the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act can be applied retroactively to pending cases. The BIPA amendment modified the law so that damages for violations can no longer be assessed on a per-scan basis, significantly reducing potential damages in biometric privacy litigation.

findings.title: Man Pleads Guilty to Violating TAKE IT DOWN Act in First-Ever Conviction
findings.summary: James Strahler II of Ohio pleaded guilty to violating the TAKE IT DOWN Act by creating AI-generated nonconsensual sexual images to threaten individuals, becoming the first person convicted under the law. U.S. Attorney Dominick Gerace II confirmed this as the first individual conviction under the act. The TAKE IT DOWN Act, signed into law in May 2025, criminalizes the publication of nonconsensual intimate imagery including AI-generated deepfakes and requires online platforms to remove reported material within 48 hours.

findings.title: US HHS Releases Guidance on HIPAA Security Rule
findings.source: IAPP U.S. Privacy Digest / Regulatory Guidance
findings.summary: The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services released guidance detailing the HIPAA Security Rule's Risk Management obligations to protect patient privacy when using digital records. HHS said organizations and healthcare providers must ensure they assess overall data security and mitigate potential risks and data protection challenges due to systems processing sensitive health information.

findings.title: DOJ Urges US Appellate Court to Rule VPPA Constitutional
findings.source: IAPP U.S. Privacy Digest / Law & Regulation
findings.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice filed a brief to the Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit in favor of upholding the constitutionality of the Video Privacy Protection Act in a First Amendment case between media company Hearst Corporation and an app user. The DOJ wrote that the VPPA is a privacy statute protecting sensitive information without regard to the content of any message in which the disclosure might be contained, and urged the court not to conclude the VPPA is unconstitutional.

findings.title: Alabama Personal Data Protection Act Signed — Details and Compliance Analysis
findings.summary: DLA Piper's Privacy Matters blog confirms Alabama became the 21st state to enact a comprehensive privacy law when House Bill 351 was signed. The Alabama Personal Data Protection Act applies to businesses controlling or processing data of more than 25,000 Alabama residents or deriving 25% of revenue from data sales, with attorney general-only enforcement and a non-sunsetting 45-day cure provision. Effective May 1, 2027, the law includes notable differences from other state laws including unique applicability thresholds and entity-level exemptions.

findings.title: Proposed State Privacy Law Update: April 6, 2026
findings.source: Troutman Pepper Locke / Privacy + Cyber + AI Blog
findings.summary: Troutman Pepper Locke's 12th weekly update on proposed state privacy legislation in 2026 covers developments including Maine's consumer data privacy bill stalling on a procedural House vote, Kentucky's legislature passing an amendment to add automatic content recognition as a category of sensitive data, and New York's Stop Online Predators Act advancing in a Senate Committee. Notable upcoming legislative deadlines include Alabama (April 16), Kansas (April 10), Kentucky (April 15), Maine (April 15), Nebraska (April 17), and Tennessee (April 24).

findings.title: Trump Executive Order Establishes National AI Policy Framework Preempting State Laws
findings.summary: President Trump signed an executive order titled 'Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence' on December 11, 2025, establishing a uniform federal AI policy that preempts state AI laws deemed inconsistent with federal policy. The order directs the Attorney General to establish an AI Litigation Task Force to challenge conflicting state AI laws, instructs the Department of Commerce to condition BEAD broadband funding on repeal of onerous state AI regulations, and directs the FTC to issue a policy statement classifying state-mandated bias mitigation as a per se deceptive trade practice by March 11, 2026.

findings.title: First Conviction Under TAKE IT DOWN Act Sets Landmark Precedent for AI Deepfakes
findings.summary: Ohio man James Strahler II became the first person in the United States convicted under the Take It Down Act, a federal law signed by President Trump in May 2025 that criminalizes the nonconsensual publication of intimate imagery including AI-generated deepfakes. Strahler pleaded guilty to three federal counts including cyberstalking, producing obscene visual representations of child sexual abuse material, and publication of digital forgeries under the TAKE IT DOWN Act. The law also requires online platforms to remove reported nonconsensual material within 48 hours.
